title: PostgreSQL replication and high availability
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: PostgreSQL writes every change to the write ahead log first.
In asynchronous replication the primary commits without waiting, so it is fast but a crash can lose the last few transactions.
Replication lag is the delay between the primary and a standby.
Patroni runs next to each PostgreSQL instance and keeps a leader key in a consensus store such as etcd.
Split brain means two nodes both accept writes.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A primary that filled its disk with retained logs
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A forgotten replica made the primary retain WAL until the disk was full.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select slot_name, active, pg_size_pretty(pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) as retai
A standby decommissioned weeks earlier still had a replication slot, so the primary kept every log segment since then.
Dropping the slot freed the space, and the team added an alert on retained WAL per slot and a step in the decommission checklist.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Forgotten replication slots.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Backups, point in time recovery and restore testing
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: A logical backup with `pg_dump` exports data as SQL and is portable across versions but slow to restore on large databases.
A base backup is a full copy of the data directory.
Point in time recovery lets you set a target such as `recovery_target_time = 2026-11-10 09:14:00`.
pgBackRest and similar tools handle full, differential and incremental backups, compression, encryption, parallel restore and retention.
Restore a backup into a scratch environment on a schedule and run integrity checks and a sample query.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: A restore that stopped at a missing segment
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
During a recovery the database refused to continue because one WAL segment was missing.
An operator runs a command such as: pgbackrest --stanza=main check
The archive command had been failing for two days because a credential expired and nobody was alerted.
The team renewed the credential, took a fresh full backup to cover the gap and added an alert on archive errors and on the age of the newest archived segment.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Treating replication as a backup.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Connection pooling and capacity
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: In PostgreSQL each connection is a process that uses memory and competes for CPU.
PgBouncer sits between applications and the database.
The number of useful active connections is roughly a small multiple of the CPU cores, often between two and four times.
`shared_buffers` is often set to about a quarter of RAM.
Watch active versus idle connections, connections waiting in the pool, query queue time, lock waits and CPU.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: Too many connections after a scale out
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Doubling the application pods made the database refuse new connections.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select state, count(*) from pg_stat_activity group by state"
Each pod kept ten idle connections and the new pods pushed the total to the limit while only 24 were doing work.
PgBouncer in transaction mode with a pool of 40 connections replaced the per pod pools, and the application settings were changed to open fewer connections.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Raising max_connections instead of pooling.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Zero downtime migrations and upgrades
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Many `ALTER TABLE` operations take an exclusive lock, and a long running query ahead of them in the queue blocks everything behind.
First expand: add the new column or table, nullable, without removing anything.
Create indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY`, which avoids blocking writes but takes longer and can leave an invalid index if it fails.
`pg_upgrade` upgrades in place quickly, especially with link mode, but needs a window and a tested rollback.
Before a risky step write the rollback.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: An index build that blocked writes for ten minutes
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A plain index creation on a busy table held a lock and orders could not be saved.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select pid, wait_event_type, query from pg_stat_activity where wait_event_type = 'Lock' limit 2"
The team created the index without CONCURRENTLY, which blocks writes for the whole build.
The next time they used CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY with a lock timeout, checked for an invalid index afterwards and scheduled it outside the peak.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Migrations with no lock timeout.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Redis and MongoDB operations
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Redis keeps data in memory. This keeps the next step safe and easy to check.
Set `maxmemory` below the machine memory with room for fork and copy on write during snapshots.
A primary with replicas can be managed by Sentinel, which monitors and promotes a replica, or by Redis Cluster, which shards keys over many primaries by hash slot.
A replica set has a primary and secondaries, and elects a new primary when it fails with a majority vote, so use three or more voting members.
Queries without an index scan the whole collection.

title: Failure and recovery: A cache that evicted the sessions
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
Users were logged out when Redis reached its memory limit and removed session keys.
An operator runs a command such as: redis-cli info memory | grep -E "used_memory_human|maxmemory_human|maxmemory_policy"
Sessions and cache entries shared one instance with an eviction policy meant for caches, so sessions were removed under pressure.
The team separated sessions into their own instance with noeviction and alerts at eighty percent memory, and left the cache with allkeys-lru.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Mixing caches and primary data in one Redis.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.

title: Database incidents and runbooks
summary: How the parts of this lesson fit together.

steps.n: Confirm the impact, check whether the database is up and accepting connections, check disk and CPU, then look at connections and the longest running queries.
In PostgreSQL `pg_stat_activity` shows running queries and their wait events, and `pg_locks` shows who blocks whom.
A full disk can stop a database.
Cancel a query with `pg_cancel_backend` before terminating it with `pg_terminate_backend`.
A good runbook starts with the symptom, lists the checks in order with exact commands, states what is safe, has a decision for each result and names who to call.
Confirm the outcome with a metric, a query or a test, and write down what changed so the next person can repeat it.

title: Failure and recovery: One idle transaction that blocked everything
summary: A realistic failure and the way back.

steps.n: The system works and the team relies on it, so nobody is watching this particular risk closely.
A forgotten transaction held a lock for six hours and queries stacked up behind it.
An operator runs a command such as: psql -c "select pid, now()-xact_start as age, state, left(query,40) from pg_stat_activity where state = 'idle
A script opened a transaction and then waited for input.
The commander cancelled it after checking it was safe, queries drained within a minute and an idle in transaction timeout was set, with an alert on the age of the oldest transaction.
The team closes the gap: avoid this mistake: Changing many things at once.
The incident is reviewed for system and process causes and the runbook is updated so the next responder finds the answer faster.
